canal_p11_001.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_001.text: The survey boat left on the twenty-fourth morning with Bao's level staff tied along the gunwale. Yue kept the sharp pegs in Tian's sewn roll instead of carrying them loose under her arm. Luo sat near the pilot, uneasy about leaving her own gate even with its named replacement. The water below the fork broadened into a slow bend fringed with yellow reeds. From this side, the canal looked less like a machine waiting for repair and more like something that had been quietly visiting other people's land.

canal_p11_002.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_002.text: The garden correspondent met them at a small landing whose last step lay under ordinary mud. She told Bao where the checked dry path began and carried her own offered sketch in a basket beside late beans. Her household had tended three beds along the old spill hollow for eleven seasons. The charter's protected wet-weather use had stayed visible in the land papers, but the channel itself had grown confused after a ridge slide. She wanted them to see what now happened there before anybody spoke as if old ink still knew every slope.

canal_p11_003.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_003.text: Luo brought the certified public-use extract and did not open it first. She asked the correspondent to show the ordinary water marks she had recorded during the last rain. They walked along the dry outer path, keeping clear of the soft hollow. A fence post held two recent marks in pencil, with dates written below. The higher old mark on the ridge came from a different bank shape. Bao checked the present marks against a fixed paving reference. Yue listened to bean leaves scraping one another in the breeze.

canal_p11_004.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_004.text: The lower stop above the gardens remained closed at the canal. Today's visit would observe ground and offered marks without sending water into it. Luo repeated that when a man called across the rows asking how soon his beans would be drowned. He had heard the word diversion and supplied its worst ending. The correspondent asked him to come to the landing after his current picking round. He agreed, still angry. Yue understood the delay as useful. An answer shouted across planted beds would begin as another piece of rumor.

canal_p11_005.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_005.text: Bao set the level instrument on stable paving and asked Yue to record the reference before he sighted toward the hollow. The original route had fallen gently toward a reed basin. The current surface dipped into an old side channel, where the ridge's slid clay made a low barrier farther on. Water reaching that dip might back toward a small house instead of continuing outward. The charter had not created the clay. It would not remove it by being read more firmly.

canal_p11_006.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_006.text: The house stood behind a low orchard wall, pale plaster flaking beside its doorway. Smoke rose from a cook pot beneath the eaves. Yue could see a strip of fresh lime along the lowest wall, too new to carry the old flood history she had imagined. The correspondent said the house had stayed dry in last week's brief shower, but a larger rain had wet its yard the previous season. The owner would return tomorrow. Today they could observe the public path without inspecting her private cut.

canal_p11_007.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_007.text: A child stood at the house gate watching Bao's staff. She asked whether it was a weapon and whether he planned to fight the canal. Bao said it measured height. The child considered that, then fetched a stick shorter than herself and announced that her family already had one. Luo knelt outside the gate and showed her the small numbers on Bao's staff. The child asked what happened after the numbers ran out. Yue laughed, grateful for a question that could not become a property claim.

canal_p11_008.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_008.text: The owner of the beans arrived with his picking basket and no intention of sitting through a lecture. He wanted to know why the canal could use his low land whenever its richer upper bank ran out of room. Luo said the seasonal hollow was a protected use, while his crops and ordinary cultivation mattered in deciding a workable present route. He asked whether mattered meant money. Yue did not answer for her. Luo said any planned disturbance needed its actual terms and source before work began.

canal_p11_009.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_009.text: His household had bought its plot with the seasonal notation intact. He admitted that after the correspondent brought the offered purchase page. He still believed decades of quiet water should have earned them a different arrangement. Bao asked him to show the portions he depended on for this season's crop. The man's anger became a walking map: beans near the ridge, late greens along the lower edge, a path needed for carrying them out. A repair could spare some rows without pretending that every row stood outside the old use.

canal_p11_010.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_010.text: At the lower hollow, the soil glittered with fragments of old roofing tile. Somebody had used broken tiles to keep the picking path firm. Bao found their edge carried over the shallow drain's intended entrance, narrowing it under ordinary dry debris. The gardener admitted he had helped place them, thinking the old hollow abandoned after the slide. He did not confess to blocking a flood he had known would come. Yue recorded the actual alteration and his offered account, which together explained a present obstruction without inventing a hidden purpose.

canal_p11_011.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_011.text: Luo wanted the tile removed immediately. Bao asked where the loose ground would shed under the next flow after that path lost its cover. The gardener said the naked edge would fall into his greens. A sound reinstatement would need the entrance opened and the walking edge supported, not merely a triumphant heap of removed fragments. Yue saw the repair growing from a cleared line into a place people had to keep using. The old use could return without making the gardener's ordinary exit impossible.

canal_p11_012.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_012.text: They ate beneath an orchard tree outside the private fence with the correspondent's permission. The pilot had brought her own rice parcel and joined them after checking the boat's mooring. Luo caught herself treating her as somebody who waited while the important visit happened. She asked when the pilot's accepted return trip had to begin. The answer left them a real afternoon interval. Bao put the longest possible walk aside for tomorrow's owner visit. The pilot opened her parcel, relieved that somebody had finally asked about her own clock.

canal_p11_013.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_013.text: Yue wrote the first survey figures while eating too quickly and dripped sauce beside a level reference. The ink stayed readable, but she copied the line to a clean field sheet and preserved the stained original in its cover. Bao said the sauce made the column look warmer. Luo said warmth would not help him read it next week. Their little argument ended with the exact numbers on both sheets, and Yue felt less afraid of being corrected by people willing to joke while they did it.

canal_p11_014.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_014.text: A woman crossing the public path recognized Pei's missing-name reference in Yue's narrow request. She did not have the receipt, but her aunt kept old seasonal papers in a tin behind the grain chest. Yue asked whether the aunt wanted the request brought to her rather than assuming the niece could offer the contents. The woman said she could ask tonight. An unfinished historical name had followed them below the fork, but it would wait while living people decided whether to open an ordinary household tin.

canal_p11_015.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_015.text: At the bend, Bao found a marker stone leaning partly out of its old socket. Its weathered face had the seasonal channel sign, and the public register placed it near this boundary. The slide had moved loose earth around it. He would not use the leaning stone alone as a precise current survey point. They measured from the stable paving reference and left the stone's old face visible without resetting it today. Yue had expected a recovered marker to make the whole afternoon easier. It gave them history and another careful question.

canal_p11_016.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_016.text: The correspondent showed Luo a shallow cut running from her washing area toward the fork. It carried ordinary household drainage during dry weather and remained outside the private cut whose owner was absent. Its small bank stood above the old hollow at one crossing. The levels suggested a flood might spill across it into the house yard unless a controlled intersection was fitted. Bao marked that as a likely route needing current design, not an observation of water they had actually released. The distinction would matter when they spoke with the owner tomorrow.

canal_p11_017.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_017.text: The bean gardener asked whether the bank would pay him to remove the tiles he had put into the seasonal entrance. Luo offered a current paid task if it entered the accepted repair order and met its remaining labor allowance. She did not promise the price before Bao measured the job. The man said he had spent unpaid hours improving the path. Yue asked whether he could show the actual cost of his materials for the later discussion. He produced a receipt tucked inside the basket handle, unexpectedly prepared for that question.

canal_p11_018.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_018.text: The tile receipt named a private purchase of discarded roofing, not a permit to change the drain. Its paid value still mattered when people discussed replacing a path he had depended on. Bao drew a narrower raised edge that might preserve the exit while reopening the channel mouth. It would use sound offcuts and ordinary gravel already assigned to the field repair if the inspection accepted them. The gardener looked less combative while examining a drawing that left his feet somewhere to stand.

canal_p11_019.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_019.text: Wind shook the orchard leaves, and a ripe pear fell just behind Luo's head. She picked it up from the public path and asked the correspondent whether it belonged to the house garden. It did. The child at the gate offered it after asking her grandmother indoors. Luo accepted the bruised fruit and cut it into shares with her household knife. Bao inspected the tree's overhanging branch, not as an engineer but as someone who preferred supper to a second pear on the crown of his head.

canal_p11_020.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_020.text: The grandmother came outside while they ate. She rented the small house and did not own the private drainage cut. Last season's yard water had reached her outdoor grain tub, costing a little millet she could describe but not prove by receipt. She wanted her experience heard before the owner spoke for the whole property. Yue wrote the offered loss with its uncertainty preserved. A person could remember a damaged tub without producing the archive evidence that settled Han's old loan.

canal_p11_021.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_021.text: Luo asked the grandmother whether anyone lived farther down the current side channel. A reed gatherer's shelter stood beyond the bend, used during cutting season. Its occupant was away at the lower landing today. The correspondent offered the ordinary contact path. Bao added the shelter to tomorrow's ground walk because the spill could reach it after passing the house. Yue had drawn the hollow as if the final reeds were empty. The first unanswered question below the fork was becoming a list of people who had not appeared on that convenient pale area.

canal_p11_022.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_022.text: The afternoon light slanted through the bean poles, making the rows look orderly from the path. Near their far edge, a shallow rut cut diagonally across the planned walking line. The pilot warned them that the dry crust could cover soft mud. Bao tested from stable ground and moved the survey route onto the higher public strip. The task took longer. The gardener complained that outsiders always walked farther than necessary. Luo told him the new route would remain marked for tomorrow's visit, and asked whether he wanted a safe crossing priced separately.

canal_p11_023.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_023.text: He said no, then changed his mind when he remembered carrying full baskets there after rain. Bao could include a small ordinary board crossing in the proposed field plan if its support was sound and materials remained available. It would not serve as a dam or carry a loaded cart. Yue wrote the actual intended foot use. The gardener asked her to draw a basket beside it so nobody later claimed he requested a bridge for trade. She added the basket in the private offered sketch and kept the service plan plain.

canal_p11_024.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_024.text: By the return time, the survey had found the current dip toward the house, the narrowed entrance and several actual receivers below it. Bao's preliminary route would need the owner's drainage visit and the shelter contact before any lower test. Luo left the offered sketch with the correspondent and kept the exact level sheet in its dry cover. The pilot called from the landing. Nobody asked her to wait until their questions grew tidy. The return boat left within its actual interval, carrying people more uncertain than when they arrived.

canal_p11_025.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_025.text: At the canal, the keeper replacement reported ordinary gate readings and a passenger dispute about a late token. The gate had worked without Luo standing beside it. She listened to his actual handling and thanked him before asking Bao about the field figures. Yue liked the order of that conversation. A familiar keeper could return without taking the day away from the person who had done it in her absence. The night reading stayed on the board under its actual observer's name.

canal_p11_026.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_026.text: The workshop reply had arrived while they were gone. A fresh qualified standby arrangement could be provided from a separate emergency appointment if the landing guild approved its relief request; no fee had been earned by sending this quote. Luo would ask the guild after comparing the forecast and current exposed work. Yue put the offered price beside future field labor. The original ninety-six repair allocation still governed planned work. A larger warning would require real additional funds before Jiang's return became part of the story.

canal_p11_027.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_027.text: On the twenty-fifth morning, the owner returned to the small house carrying a parcel of seed bought upriver. She accepted the previously proposed visit and invited them to inspect her actual drainage cut from the dry edge. The reed gatherer also agreed to meet at his shelter. Pei's possible receipt contact had sent word that her aunt would open the tin after her morning meal. Three different paths could deepen the current survey: the private cut, the occupied lower hollow or the old receiving reference beside it.

canal_p11_028.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_028.text: Bao would lead the private-cut level comparison, Luo would hear the reed shelter's present use, and a permitted household visit could pursue the counterfoil without searching beyond its offered scope. Each team would return to the house landing before the planned design discussion. Yue chose where her own attention could change the next conversation. Yesterday's map had not lied so much as left people out. Today there was time to meet some of them before water made their absence impossible to ignore.

canal_p11_029.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_029.text: The accepted visits stood on three pieces of paper with three different times. Yue could examine the private cut with Bao, walk the lower shelter route with Luo or hear the aunt's offered receiving history. The main design would wait for all current ground reports. The historical inquiry could leave its name unanswered without blocking that design. Yue would hear one set of answers closely and receive the others from people whose own eyes deserved to remain part of the account.

choices.text: Examine the household cut with Bao.
Walk the occupied lower hollow with Luo.
Hear the aunt's offered receiving history.

canal_p11_030.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_030.text: Bao met the owner beside her washing bench after she cleared the jars. Yue introduced herself without opening the old charter across the woman's seed parcel. The owner said she had cut the small drainage channel three seasons earlier because surface water collected against her back wall. A local builder had helped, and she kept his drawing. The cut relieved her own yard under ordinary rain. She did not know it could meet a reopened spill route carrying a very different volume.

canal_p11_031.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_031.text: The builder's drawing showed the small channel's intended dry-weather slope toward the fork, with a short retaining lip at its intersection. Bao compared that lip with the current ground and found part of it buried by loose clay from the slide. The owner had thought the deposit harmless because her washing water still left. He asked her to show its ordinary outlet while Yue recorded the accessible heights. They did not pour test water into the old seasonal route to make a more dramatic explanation.

canal_p11_032.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_032.text: At the intersection, a narrow erosion notch crossed the retaining lip. Its exposed edge looked newer than the covered builder's mark. Bao could not date it exactly from its color, but last season's offered photograph did not exist; the owner had only a hand sketch and her memory. Yue nearly wrote that the notch must have formed after the larger rain. She crossed out the inference and kept the actual worn shape. The repair proposal could address today's opening without inventing the day it began.

canal_p11_033.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_033.text: The owner asked whether the canal would remove her private cut. Bao said the ordinary household outlet could remain if the seasonal crossing regained a controlled lip and the new spill guide kept its tested head within the route's limit. That design still needed a current downstream check. She wanted a drawing that showed both waters, not one blue line swallowing another. Yue made separate arrows on the offered plan. It took longer than drawing a channel everyone could pretend meant the same thing.

canal_p11_034.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_034.text: The grandmother brought tea to the outer table and said the owner had never heard about the wet grain tub. They had spoken after the rain, but each remembered the other's concern as something already answered. The owner looked hurt, then asked to hear the loss again. Yue stood aside while the women described different parts of that evening. One had hurried to arrange a builder; the other had wanted help lifting food. Neither account disappeared when they discovered both could be true.

canal_p11_035.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_035.text: The owner offered to replace the remembered millet from her own household store. The grandmother accepted only the quantity she believed lost and asked for a smaller high shelf instead of a prettier tub. Its material and fitting would be the owner's separate private work, not a public repair item. Yue wrote the offered agreement at their request. The old loss still lacked a precise receiving receipt, but two people could make an ordinary settlement without requiring the canal to certify every remembered kernel.

canal_p11_036.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_036.text: Bao measured the accessible side of the cut from stable ground. A buried outlet lay beyond the present view. The owner wanted him to pull off its old cover immediately because she had finally agreed to the visit. He checked the support drawing and explained that the cover rested near a loaded wall pier. The qualified mason would assess it before opening. Permission made inspection possible; it did not turn the carpenter into someone trained to decide a buried wall's safe load.

canal_p11_037.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_037.text: She laughed with sudden embarrassment and said she had called every person carrying a tool a builder. Bao said people called him a cultivator when he carried Jiang's empty case. Yue said people called her an official when she copied a line neatly. The grandmother asked whether any of them was useful at mending a kettle handle. Bao raised his hand before thinking, then inspected the kettle on the table as an ordinary small favor after the survey pause. The afternoon gained one task no charter had predicted.

canal_p11_038.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_038.text: A broken tie beneath the handle let the kettle tilt dangerously when full. Bao fitted a temporary household cord only after checking the intact metal loop, and told the grandmother to keep its ordinary fill low until her regular repairer replaced the missing tie. The owner set aside personal repair money for that job too. Yue watched tea served from the steadier pot. Care at a household table could be modest and still change the next hour. Nobody needed to rename it a canal duty.

canal_p11_039.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_039.text: At the landing discussion, Bao presented the cut's actual crossing, the buried lip and the uninspected outlet near the wall. Yue brought the two women's private millet-and-shelf agreement only to its agreed receiver, outside the public repair plan. The owner asked for the proposed spill crossing to preserve her ordinary drainage wherever the current checks allowed it. The design now had a person able to approve real work on her ground, and a limit nobody could erase by calling the whole place a flood problem.

canal_p11_040.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_040.text: Luo walked the lower public strip with Yue while the reed gatherer led them to his shelter. Its roof was a patchwork of old sailcloth, held low against wind. He slept there during cutting season because taking bundles home each evening cost more than he earned. The shelter stood on a permitted seasonal camp patch beside the hollow. He had been told the channel would never run that far again. Luo asked who told him. He named a former bank worker, whose confidence had not changed the current use in the register.

canal_p11_041.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_041.text: The gatherer did not want to argue about the old worker. He wanted somewhere to sleep if the channel reopened. A higher public rest shed near the landing had room for one temporary bed while his camp stayed exposed. Its receiver would need to accept the arrangement and keep the ordinary passage clear. Luo sent the actual request through the landing contact rather than promising a building she did not manage. Yue helped the man identify which of his things could move easily and which would need a cart.

canal_p11_042.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_042.text: His heaviest item was a hand cutter fixed to an old timber base. He had shaped it himself and disliked the thought of leaving it in the hollow. Bao's field plan did not include a private equipment transport service. Luo asked the gatherer whether the landing's ordinary small cart fare was affordable. He said it would consume two mornings' better reed price. Yue felt ready to pay it for him, then heard Luo ask whether the shed receiver's relief allowance covered exposed seasonal workers. A durable answer might exist beyond her purse.

canal_p11_043.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_043.text: The receiver's reply came through a passing porter: one accepted temporary displacement could use the shed's own small relocation allowance, with the actual cart journey and bed space recorded. The gatherer would be its recipient, not a canal repair worker in disguise. He accepted the move after checking when his own cutter could return. Yue wrote the camp's current vulnerable position in the field report. The relocation made a person safer without pretending the whole flood route had now been accepted.

canal_p11_044.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_044.text: They followed the higher strip beyond the shelter, where reeds leaned over a shallow basin. The gatherer showed ordinary water marks on a fixed stone post from two recent rain seasons. Bao's level work would still decide the current route. Luo thanked him for a useful local record and asked how he kept the dates. He laughed and showed tally cuts made for his own reed harvests. The dates had stayed useful because somebody needed them before the canal arrived with a question.

canal_p11_045.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_045.text: A hidden depression interrupted the higher strip. Yue saw a dry reed mat covering it and thought it was a walking board. The gatherer stopped her at the edge and pushed his pole through the mat into soft ground. He had left it there to keep harvested reeds from lying in mud, not to provide a crossing. Yue stepped back onto the established path. Her fourth-stage cord offered no better footing. Luo moved the survey line around the depression and marked it where tomorrow's crew could see the actual interruption.

canal_p11_046.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_046.text: The gatherer asked whether the canal could hire him to guide the later clearing because he knew the reed basin. Luo said she could offer that knowledge in the current hiring plan, with an actual task and available funding. He wanted one short morning, not an open-ended call whenever weather worried the bank. Yue wrote his availability and the ordinary work he could explain. His offered local knowledge might help the later crew. It did not oblige him to return from his bed whenever someone shouted for the old shelter's occupant.

canal_p11_047.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_047.text: At the basin's far lip, a discarded fish trap blocked the small return channel. It belonged to a landing family whose name was marked on the frame. Luo notified the receiver and asked for removal before any bounded field test. The gatherer wanted to break it because he disliked its owner. Yue said a blocked path could be cleared through the actual notice and ordinary timing unless immediate danger required another action. There was no live flow today. His annoyance stayed an opinion beside a useful reported obstruction.

canal_p11_048.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_048.text: The trap's owner arrived after hearing the message and denied placing it there. He recognized his repair mark but said a flood had taken it from the landing. Nobody had evidence of his deliberate blocking. He agreed to recover it with his own light cart before the next ground check. The gatherer watched silently, then helped show the dry route because he preferred seeing the trap leave to prolonging their old quarrel. Yue recorded the cleared obstruction after it actually reached the cart.

canal_p11_049.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_049.text: Luo returned to the landing with the shelter relocation accepted, the soft depression marked and the return channel clear of the recovered trap. The gatherer would move his bed before any lower flow trial and keep his temporary shed space under its actual terms. Yue had heard his impatience, his fear and his useful knowledge without requiring them to become one friendly attitude. The larger route now ended at an occupied basin with a real exit, rather than the empty reeds she had first drawn.

canal_p11_050.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_050.text: The aunt opened her tin after the morning meal and invited Yue to sit near the window. Her niece stayed only until the offered papers were arranged. The tin contained household receipts, a wedding note and a private letter whose fold the aunt left untouched. Yue repeated the exterior reference and season from Pei's narrow request. The aunt found a matching counterfoil beneath an old cookery list. Its final mark differed from the misleading lead already rejected at the canal. This one would need comparison at the actual receiving page.

canal_p11_051.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_051.text: The aunt said the worked turns belonged to her older sister Qiao Lan, who had moved across the fork after marrying. The public receiving copy had scratched through a former household name during that move. Yue asked why the counterfoil stayed in this tin. Qiao Lan had left it here while the new house roof leaked, then died before collecting every paper. The aunt wanted the actual name restored, but would not lend the original away. An approved copy could travel with the offered exterior reference.

canal_p11_052.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_052.text: Yue copied the legible parts while the aunt watched. The old ink had darkened around one day notation, leaving the accepted seasonal reference clear but its full tally less easy. The collective season had already been certified complete. This inquiry would concern personal attribution rather than renew anybody's labor. The aunt said she understood and asked Yue to write Qiao Lan's chosen name instead of the shortened household label used by the old clerk. Yue set the pen down until she could hear the spelling slowly.

canal_p11_053.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_053.text: The aunt corrected the third character after Yue wrote it. She said Qiao Lan had changed the form herself, and people kept returning the old one out of habit. Yue wrote the approved name again on the offered copy and left the corrected first attempt visible in her field notes. A recovered history could still be damaged by the person eager to restore it quickly. The aunt laughed when Yue looked too solemn and asked whether she wanted another cup of tea before trying to save the rest of the world.

canal_p11_054.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_054.text: Qiao Lan had liked the founding work song because she could make other workers laugh with its verses. The aunt also remembered her coming home too tired to cook after the last turn. Yue did not ask which memory represented her true opinion. The woman in the story had been able to enjoy a tune and resent a burden. The aunt wanted both sentences beside the restored name if a public history used her offered account. She approved their wording after Yue read it back.

canal_p11_055.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_055.text: The niece returned carrying a broken bowl wrapped in cloth. She had thought the seasonal number might be marked on its base because her mother used it to keep small papers dry. The aunt shook her head; the bowl carried only a potter's sign. Yue resisted connecting every old object to the found receipt. The niece laughed at her own hope and asked whether the bowl could be mended. It had a clean break. They set it aside for the ordinary pottery repairer, whose craft could give it a future unrelated to the missing name.

canal_p11_056.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_056.text: Through the window, they could see the proposed spill strip beyond the bean plots. The aunt remembered crossing it on a plank as a young woman before the slide altered its far bank. Her remembered route joined the old charter but did not establish today's levels. Yue asked whether she would show its former landing from the public path if her knees allowed. The aunt preferred to mark it on the offered sketch. Her niece would show the actual current place without asking an older body to verify an old story by walking it.

canal_p11_057.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_057.text: The niece led Yue along the higher path after the visit. The former plank landing remained visible as an old stone notch, now above the shallow side dip. Bao could compare that location with his current reference. Yue wrote the aunt's memory date beside its source and kept the visible stone separate from the remembered crossing. The niece said outsiders always wanted her family to know exactly what old water had done. Yue told her today's new route would need measurements from people paid to make them.

canal_p11_058.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_058.text: At the landing, Yue gave the approved counterfoil copy and name request their own dry cover. The aunt's original stayed in its tin, and the private letter stayed folded. Luo received the old crossing location as offered history, with a current survey still required. The niece took the public-use extract home at her aunt's request. She wanted to read it beside the former seasonal receipt so the family could understand both what had ended and what remained. Yue gave her the actual document, not a conclusion about how she ought to feel.

canal_p11_059.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_059.text: Yue sent Pei a message describing the offered matching exterior reference before the original copy journey. The actual attribution remained pending comparison against the public receiving page. The aunt would receive the result through her chosen niece rather than an unexpected public announcement. The visit had found a promising paper and an actual person's chosen name. It had also heard a work song beside exhaustion. Yue returned to the design discussion feeling how much richer an answer could become when it stopped demanding one clean emotion.

canal_p11_060.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_060.text: The afternoon reports met at the house landing. Bao's private-cut levels, Luo's lower shelter walk and the aunt's offered historical lead arrived through their actual observers. Yue understood one set most closely and listened carefully to the others. The private outlet near the wall still needed a qualified mason's assessment. The reed shelter had an accepted temporary relocation before flow. The historical name remained pending comparison. None of those facts could stand in for the current levels that would decide where their water safely went.

canal_p11_061.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_061.text: Bao's preliminary design used the reopened seasonal entrance, a supported picking path and a fitted lip above the household cut. A public outer strip could guide flow toward the basin without crossing the planted beans. The current dip and clay barrier needed modest reshaping inside that protected route. With the chair's authorization, the clerk reassigned an unstarted carpentry half-day to the masonry assessment and changed Bao's remaining sequence. Luo asked for actual quantities before calling the design accepted. A buried fault could still require another plan.

canal_p11_062.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_062.text: The garden owner wanted the fitted lip to include a hand-close board so ordinary household drainage could remain separate outside flood use. Bao could design that small board within the remaining field fittings, but it would have its own checked operating head. It would not be a second flood gate capable of holding the whole canal. Yue drew its intended position and movement. The owner accepted the current proposal for further assessment, then asked who would check it when the canal keeper was busy with boats.

canal_p11_063.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_063.text: Luo proposed a named local observer during any planned lower trial, with the actual paid task arranged before live flow. The owner wanted to choose whether to take that job. If she declined, another qualified observer could stand on the agreed public strip without occupying her yard. The bean gardener objected that this would cost more than a household turn. Bao asked him whether his basket could carry a worker who had never arrived. He muttered, but later offered a short task clearing his own reachable tile entrance for the listed rate.

canal_p11_064.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_064.text: The reed gatherer arrived to say his bed had actually reached the higher shed. The cutter's cart journey had passed the ordinary check, and its receiving note belonged to the shed allowance. He brought the empty lamp from his shelter so nobody later mistook it for a sign that a person still slept in the hollow. Luo marked the relocation complete. A future flow test would still require the basin and return path checked anew. An emptied bed was an actual change, not a permanent promise that the hollow contained nobody.

canal_p11_065.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_065.text: On the twenty-sixth morning, the qualified mason met them at the private cut's covered outlet. His half-day came from the formally reassigned field interval; his earlier gate finishing day was already complete. He checked the loaded wall pier and accepted a careful cover opening from the dry side without removing structural support. The accessible outlet showed sound pipe beyond a small sediment shelf. Its cleaning could proceed within this agreed task. A buried structural problem had remained possible, but today's actual view did not find one.

canal_p11_066.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_066.text: The mason cleared the reachable sediment and reset the cover on its proper support. The household's ordinary outlet then ran under the owner's small jar test, with that test water kept out of the seasonal hollow. Bao compared the restored outlet height against his spill plan. The fitted crossing could preserve this path if its current limits held. Yue watched the owner smile at water leaving her yard, then grow serious again at the drawing of water arriving elsewhere. Relief about one route did not remove concern about the other.

canal_p11_067.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_067.text: The gardener began lifting the reachable tiles from the seasonal entrance during his accepted short task. He kept the good fragments in his own basket after the public opening was clear, rather than treating them as canal material automatically. Bao laid out the supported foot edge on the existing sound ground. The narrow crossing served people carrying baskets and had its limit marked before anyone tried a cart. Yue helped sweep loose sharp pieces from the walking line. The reopened mouth no longer depended on people pretending they did not use the path beside it.

canal_p11_068.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_068.text: The remaining field timber came from the ordinary second stock length already assigned to the spill preparation. Bao fitted the small crossing board and guide lip while the mason checked its accessible seating. The current live lower trial remained unscheduled until the whole repaired route and observers were accepted. No powered frame was used without Jiang's fresh appointment. Yue's opened routes stayed at their recovered second-pair baseline. Her most useful hand that morning held the ordinary square steady while Bao marked where the timber actually needed cutting.

canal_p11_069.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_069.text: A shallow old clay pot lay under the removed tiles, broken into several harmless pieces. The gardener said his youngest child had buried it while playing at a market store. Yue had been ready to think it another remnant of founding work. She handed the pieces to the child after checking their edges with the parent. He was delighted that his forgotten shop had been excavated. Luo said the canal had enough old accounts without collecting his imaginary debts too. The gardener smiled despite himself.

canal_p11_070.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_070.text: The repaired outer strip met the basin at a narrow turn. Bao wanted its flow widened gradually through a shallow spreader rather than concentrated against the soft lip. The current public-use width permitted that shaping. It would require careful observation before any large seasonal use, and the upper pocket's small response acceptance could not certify it. Yue wrote a proposed lower low-flow test with its actual feeder limit and stopping receivers. The design had become more useful by surrendering the illusion that every part could be accepted on the same afternoon.

canal_p11_071.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_071.text: Luo sent the current field quantities to the canal clerk. Remaining ordinary worker hours and materials still covered this modest shaping and finishing. A future emergency would have its own source; the workshop standby request remained a quote. The owner asked whether the bank could promise no garden loss in any flood. Luo said she could promise the defined present repair and actual response procedure, then show where uncertainty remained. The gardener said that sounded discouraging. His correspondent said an encouraging guarantee would not make the ridge stop shedding clay.

canal_p11_072.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_072.text: The first shared walk along the repaired dry route included the owner, her tenant, the bean gardener and the reed gatherer. Bao pointed out the current ground retreat toward the higher landing, which did not cross the soft depression. They could follow it in ordinary boots without entering the hollow. The grandmother wanted a resting place halfway if she had to leave. The landing receiver offered the stable orchard-wall bench, with its owner approving temporary emergency use. Yue checked its actual position on the new sketch rather than drawing a vague arrow uphill.

canal_p11_073.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_073.text: The grandmother sat there for a minute and asked whether she could bring her grain tub if warning came. Bao said the response should bring people first and move goods only while the checked route stayed open and there was actual time. She said millet felt personal too. Yue understood, then asked her to choose a light covered sack she could keep ready without carrying the tub. They found one in the house store. The arrangement did not make leaving painless, but it gave her hands something possible.

canal_p11_074.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_074.text: At the landing, the niece delivered the aunt's approved counterfoil copy into its dated courier cover. The canal clerk would receive it before Pei's next public comparison. The niece wanted the eventual personal name read at home first if verified. Yue recorded that request and kept the family history outside the hydraulic plan. The two tasks had traveled together because people lived beside water, not because every old receipt could tell them how a new board should fit.

canal_p11_075.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_075.text: The return boat carried Bao's current drawing, Luo's observer proposals and a small jar of beans sold by the gardener at his ordinary price. Yue bought it for her own supper rather than accepting it as payment for explaining the charter. The gardener still disliked the seasonal use and wanted the later test stopped if it touched his protected rows. That condition stayed visible. Friendship did not have to precede a workable arrangement, and a paid jar of beans could remain simply a good jar of beans.

canal_p11_076.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_076.text: At the canal, Tian met Yue on the flour-store stair with a stitching order spread over one knee. She asked how many new gates Bao had found by visiting one old hollow. Yue said one little board, one crossing and more people than she had expected. Tian said this was why she priced sail repairs by actually opening the seam. They ate the beans with a little barley after Tian put away the customer's cloth. Yue told her about the child's buried market pot, leaving private household accounts out of their supper.

canal_p11_077.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_077.text: Pei accepted the offered counterfoil copy and matching exterior reference from the courier. She would compare the chosen personal name against the scratched-through line in the public receiving schedule on the next agreed counter morning. The old collective labor remained discharged meanwhile. Han inspected the reserved hoist after hearing that the lower route was moving toward repair. His private sixteen-copper receiving payment still depended on delivery on day forty. Both unanswered matters had real next steps. Neither needed to interrupt a tenant's newly cleared yard.

canal_p11_078.speaker: narrator
canal_p11_078.text: Before sleep, Yue set the current route drawing beside the old charter extract. Their lines agreed only after several small changes in timber, path and expectation. The protected use had given the bank a reason to ask about the hollow. People and ground had given that use somewhere it might actually work. On the twenty-seventh morning, they would return to the small house beside the spill for its low-flow preparation, and hear what a tenant needed before the canal could call her departure route ready.
